QAM-W: Joint 2D Codebook Quantization for LLM Weights via Hadamard Rotation and Activation-Aware Scaling

Preetam Sharma Affiliation: Independent Research Email: preetam@manifoldlab.ai    Kacper Dobek Affiliation: Institute of Computing Science Affiliation: Poznan University of Technology, Poznan, Poland Email: kacper.dobek@cs.put.poznan.pl
Abstract

Scalar post-training quantizers discard pairwise coordinate structure within weight rows. We introduce QAM-W (Quadrature Amplitude Modulation for Weights), a codec that recovers this structure: each row is L2-normalized, block-Hadamard rotated, paired into 2D coordinates, and quantized against a single Lloyd-Max codebook trained on the unit circular Gaussian, with activation-aware per-channel scaling. In a cross-model study spanning five LLMs from four families (1.1B–13B parameters) and eight quantized configurations, the activation-aware variant at ≈5.5\approx 5.5 bpw stays within ±0.4%\pm 0.4\% of BF16 WikiText-2 perplexity on every model, matching the SmoothQuant W8A8 quality envelope at 32%32\% fewer weight bits. Joint 2D coding outperforms polar (amplitude ×\times phase) coding by 2–15 pp Δ\DeltaPPL at equal bitrate, and paired KL against BF16 tracks Δ\DeltaPPL% at Spearman ρ=0.99\rho=0.99 across 37 (method, model) rows, consistent with a monotone composite bound from codec distortion to KL divergence. A 3.5 bpw variant is competitive on quantization-tolerant architectures. At strict 4 bpw, the rotated-codebook frontier method QTIP outperforms QAM-W; the contribution is the quality-preserving 5–6 bpw band.

1 Introduction

Most post-training quantizers in current use are scalar: each weight is mapped independently to a small integer index, with per-group or per-channel scales. Scalar coding is simple but leaves rate-distortion slack for sources whose coordinates are correlated. Within a weight row, coordinates are typically correlated; after an orthogonal rotation they approximate a 2D circular Gaussian. Quantizing pairs jointly – as points in the plane rather than as two independent scalars – recovers pair-level structure that a scalar codebook discards.

The empirical claim of this work is bounded: in the ≈5\approx 5–66 bpw quality-preserving regime, an activation-aware joint-2D codec stays within ±0.4%\pm 0.4\% of BF16 perplexity across five LLMs from four families spanning 1.11.1B–1313B parameters, matching SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2023) W8A8’s quality at ≈32%\approx 32\% fewer weight bits. At strict 44 bpw, QTIP (Tseng et al., 2024b) outperforms QAM-W (section 5.2); the contribution here is the 5–6 bpw band.

Rotation-based methods such as QuIP (Chee et al., 2023) and QuIP# (Tseng et al., 2024a) apply incoherent rotations to homogenize coordinate magnitudes before scalar or lattice coding. Activation-aware methods such as AWQ (Lin et al., 2024) exploit the per-channel activation scale but leave joint coordinate structure untouched. The codec presented here combines all three ideas: a deterministic block-Hadamard rotation, joint 2D Lloyd-Max coding against a single codebook trained on the unit circular Gaussian (Lloyd, 1982), and AWQ-style per-channel scaling driven by the layer-output trace identity.

Throughout, reported bits-per-weight (bpw) refers to weight-storage and memory-bandwidth footprint. The current pipeline dequantizes to BF16 before matmul; latency claims would require a fused kernel and are out of scope (see Limitations).

Contributions:
  • •

    Codec and analysis. A row-norm-factored, block-Hadamard-rotated, joint 2D Lloyd-Max codec for LLM weights with activation-aware scaling, backed by a composite monotone bound from codec distortion to KL divergence (sections 3 and 4).

  • •

    Cross-model study. Eight quantized configurations on five LLMs under a unified perplexity, paired-KL, and six-task harness protocol (sections 5.1 and 5.2).

  • •

    KL as rank diagnostic. Across 3737 (method, model) rows, paired KL and Δ\DeltaPPL% are rank-correlated at Spearman ρ=0.99\rho=0.99.

2 Related Work

Scalar post-training quantization.

Round-to-nearest (RTN) quantization (Krishnamoorthi, 2018) with per-group scaling is the simplest baseline. GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023) compensates quantization error column-by-column using approximate second-order information. AWQ (Lin et al., 2024) protects high-activation channels via per-channel scaling; AutoRound (Cheng et al., 2023) refines rounding with SignSGD; HQQ (Badri and Shaji, 2023) treats rounding as a half-quadratic problem without calibration data. SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2023) redistributes quantization difficulty from activations to weights through a diagonal scaling transform, targeting joint W8A8. OmniQuant (Shao et al., 2024) jointly learns clipping and smoothing transforms. LLM.int8() (Dettmers et al., 2022) keeps outlier activation channels in 16-bit mixed precision. SqueezeLLM (Kim et al., 2024) couples a non-uniform scalar codebook with a dense-and-sparse decomposition; QLoRA’s NF4 (Dettmers et al., 2023) places levels on the Gaussian distribution.

Rotated and vector quantization.

QuIP (Chee et al., 2023) and QuIP# (Tseng et al., 2024a) apply random or structured orthogonal rotations to decorrelate weight coordinates before quantization. QuaRot (Ashkboos et al., 2024) extends rotation through the residual stream for end-to-end 4-bit inference; SpinQuant (Liu et al., 2025) replaces the fixed rotation with a learned one. QAM-W shares the rotation principle but opts for a deterministic block-Hadamard, which requires no calibration on the rotation itself. Iso-bpw comparison against the learned-rotation family is deferred to future work.

On the VQ side, AQLM (Egiazarian et al., 2024) uses additive codebooks and pushes below 2.52.5 bpw. QTIP (Tseng et al., 2024b) combines an E8E_{8}-lattice trellis with Hadamard incoherence and is the strongest published rotated-codebook method; it and QAM-W occupy different operating points, with QTIP stronger at strict 4 bpw and QAM-W stronger in the 5–6 bpw band (section 5.2). VPTQ (Liu et al., 2024) stacks residual codebooks down to ∼2\sim\!2 bpw; GPTVQ (van Baalen et al., 2024) shows the rate-distortion gain from higher codebook dimension saturates around d=8d\!=\!8, placing QAM-W’s d=2d\!=\!2 choice at the small end of that spectrum by design.

Concurrent work.

PolarQuant (Vicentino, 2026) couples a Walsh-Hadamard rotation with a scalar (d=1d\!=\!1) Lloyd-Max codebook, sharing QAM-W’s first two pipeline stages but differing in codebook dimension. The d=1d\!=\!1 vs. d=2d\!=\!2 ablation is the highest-priority follow-up.

Signal-processing origins.

Quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) originates in digital communications (Proakis and Salehi, 2008); QAM-W adapts this geometric view to weight compression. The codebook training follows the Lloyd-Max tradition (Lloyd, 1982; Max, 1960) extended to 2D sources, and can be seen as a Hadamard-rotated generalization of the kk-means weight clustering in Deep Compression (Han et al., 2016).

3 QAM-W Codec Pipeline

This section describes the codec as an encoder/decoder pair. The mathematical properties of the rotation and polar baseline are separated into appendix A.

3.1 Encoder

QAM-W quantizes a weight matrix W∈ℝdout×dinW\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times d_{\mathrm{in}}} row-by-row. For each row ww, the encoder performs the following steps:

  1. 1.

    Separate scale from direction. Record the row norm r=‖w‖2r=\|w\|_{2} as separate metadata and normalize the row to u=w/ru=w/r when r>0r>0. If r=0r=0, the row is encoded as a zero row.

  2. 2.

    Rotate the direction. Apply a deterministic sign-masked block-Hadamard rotation, giving y=Rfwd​uy=R_{\mathrm{fwd}}u.

  3. 3.

    Pair coordinates. Group adjacent rotated coordinates into complex values zk=y2​k+i​y2​k+1z_{k}=y_{2k}+iy_{2k+1} for k=0,…,d/2−1k=0,\ldots,d/2-1.

  4. 4.

    Normalize each pair. Divide each pair by its calibrated scale σk\sigma_{k}.

  5. 5.

    Quantize. Encode each normalized pair either with the polar baseline codebooks or with the joint 2D QAM-W codebook.

  6. 6.

    Pack. Store the resulting codebook indices in a bit-packed byte stream.

3.2 Decoder

The decoder reverses the encoder: unpack codebook indices, look up the corresponding centroids, rescale each pair by σk\sigma_{k}, reassemble pairs into a rotated real vector, apply the inverse rotation RinvR_{\mathrm{inv}}, and multiply by the stored row norm rr. The benchmark charges 16 bits per row for norm metadata; a fully serialized f16 row norm would add a small radial quantization term not part of the directional analysis in appendix A.

3.3 Rotation Choice

The rotation used by the encoder is a block-Hadamard transform with a deterministic sign mask. It is cheap to apply with a butterfly algorithm and requires no stored dense matrix. The implementation chooses the block size bb as the largest power of two dividing the row dimension dind_{\text{in}}, capped at bmax=1024b_{\max}=1024. For the weight matrices in the experiments in this paper, din=2048d_{\text{in}}=2048 uses b=1024b=1024 and din=5632d_{\text{in}}=5632 uses b=512b=512. The rotation’s exact isometry property is proved in lemma 1.

3.4 Pair Calibration

After rotation, adjacent coordinates are modeled empirically as approximately circular Gaussian pairs with pair-specific scale σk\sigma_{k}. Under the idealized model that the two coordinates in pair kk are zero-mean Gaussian variables with equal variance σk2\sigma_{k}^{2} and zero covariance, the amplitude |zk||z_{k}| is Rayleigh distributed and 𝔼​|zk|=σk​π/2\mathbb{E}|z_{k}|=\sigma_{k}\sqrt{\pi/2}. Calibration therefore estimates

σ^k=mean⁡(|zk|)π/2\hat{\sigma}_{k}=\frac{\operatorname{mean}(|z_{k}|)}{\sqrt{\pi/2}} (1)

from up to 1024 unit-normalized rows per weight matrix.

3.5 Polar Baseline

The polar baseline quantizes amplitude and phase independently. The amplitude |zk|/σk|z_{k}|/\sigma_{k} is quantized with an Na=2BaN_{a}=2^{B_{a}} level Lloyd-Max codebook for the unit Rayleigh density f(r)=re−r2/2f(r)=re^{-r^{2}/2}. The phase arg⁡(zk)\arg(z_{k}) is rounded to one of Np=2BpN_{p}=2^{B_{p}} uniform bins. The total per-pair budget is B=Ba+BpB=B_{a}+B_{p} bits. The pairwise distortion model for this baseline is analyzed in theorem 1.

3.6 Joint 2D QAM

The main QAM-W variant replaces the two independent polar codebooks with a single 2D codebook 𝒞={c0,…,c2B−1}⊂ℝ2\mathcal{C}=\{c_{0},\ldots,c_{2^{B}-1}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}. The codebook is trained by Lloyd iterations on the unit circular Gaussian

f⁡(x,y)=12​π​exp⁡(−x2+y22).f(x,y)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\exp\left(-\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{2}\right). (2)

Encoding maps each normalized pair zk/σkz_{k}/\sigma_{k} to its nearest codebook entry by Euclidean distance. Decoding is a table lookup followed by multiplication by σk\sigma_{k}.

The current experiments use B=11B=11 bits per pair, matching the 5+65{+}6 polar configuration in nominal pair payload. Native byte alignment and stream layout can differ between polar and joint-2D implementations; the comparison is therefore equal-bits-per-pair rather than byte-identical storage.

The choice d=2d=2 is also deliberate at the decode end: reconstruction is a single lookup into a 2B2^{B}-entry table that, at B≤11B\leq 11, occupies at most 1616 KB and stays L1-resident. This is structurally simpler than the multi-codebook lookups and vector additions of additive methods such as AQLM (Egiazarian et al., 2024), or the sequential trellis decoding of QTIP (Tseng et al., 2024b). Given that rate-distortion gains saturate by d≈8d\approx 8 (section 2), d=2d=2 deliberately trades part of the asymptotic ceiling for a decode path that is one cache-resident table read.

3.7 Bitrate Accounting

The bitrate per weight includes BB bits per pair for the codebook index and 16 bits per row for row-norm metadata. Since each pair covers two scalar coordinates,

bpw=B2+16din.\operatorname{bpw}=\frac{B}{2}+\frac{16}{d_{\mathrm{in}}}. (3)

For din=2048d_{\mathrm{in}}=2048 and B=11B=11, this is approximately 5.51 bpw before byte-alignment overhead. Reported bitrates include the row-level packing and alignment used by the implementation.

3.8 The QAM-W-3.5 Low-Bit Variant

To probe the sub-4 bpw regime, QAM-W is instantiated with B=7B=7 bits per pair, giving a 27=1282^{7}=128-entry 2D Lloyd-Max codebook trained on the same unit circular Gaussian. Activation-aware per-channel scaling (appendix B) remains applicable. For din=2048d_{\mathrm{in}}=2048 the per-pair budget plus row-norm metadata gives bpw≈3.51\operatorname{bpw}\approx 3.51; the AWQ-aware variant adds ∼0.003\sim 0.003 bpw of per-channel scale metadata for α=0.3\alpha=0.3. This is the configuration analyzed in section 5.3.1.

4 Analysis

QAM-W’s design rests on four analytical results. We state them here and defer the formal statements, proofs, and supporting empirical checks to appendices A, B and C.

The rotation is distortion-free.

The sign-masked block-Hadamard rotation is an exact isometry in real arithmetic (lemma 1): it adds no reconstruction error and only redistributes energy within each block before quantization. It does not by itself make the rotated coordinates Gaussian; that the post-rotation complex pairs concentrate near a circular Gaussian is an empirical property, checked by QQ plots against fitted Rayleigh and Gaussian marginals (section A.4).

Joint 2D coding dominates polar at fixed rate.

For the polar baseline, the per-pair distortion splits into an amplitude term and a phase term with a closed form under the Rayleigh–Lloyd source model (theorems 1 and 1). Because that factorization codes amplitude and phase independently, it cannot capture the pair-level correlation that a single 2D codebook exploits.

Activation-weighted error is the right objective.

The layer-output error obeys the trace identity ‖X​Δ​W⊤‖F2=Tr⁡(Δ​W​M^x​Δ​W⊤)\|X\Delta W^{\top}\|_{F}^{2}=\operatorname{Tr}(\Delta W\hat{M}_{x}\Delta W^{\top}) (proposition B.1), so what a quantized layer actually contributes is activation-weighted error, not raw weight MSE. This motivates AWQ-style per-channel scaling, which attenuates the contribution of high-RMS input channels under a diagonal-MxM_{x} model (corollaries 3 and B.2). Empirically, the amplification of weight-domain Frobenius error into layer-output RMSE varies by 0.550.55–5.5×5.5\times across layers and methods (table 4).

A monotone codec-to-KL bound.

Chaining the rotation isometry, the pairwise identity, the layer-output trace identity, and a softmax-Fisher local KL expansion (corollary 4) yields an upper bound on the paired KL between the BF16 and quantized models that is monotone in two scalars: the per-pair Lloyd distortion DBD_{B} (codec) and a model-fixed constant CWC_{W} (theorem 2). The bound motivates, but does not prove, that realized KL should rank methods the same way DBD_{B} does; across the 3737 (method, model) rows in this study, paired KL and Δ\DeltaPPL% are rank-correlated at Spearman ρ=0.99\rho=0.99 (fig. 1).

5 Experiments

Eight quantized configurations are evaluated against a BF16 reference on three instruction-tuned LLMs: TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat (Zhang et al., 2024), Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024), and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (Jiang et al., 2023). These are dense decoder-only transformers with standard attention, chosen so the comparison rests on mature, audited loading and evaluation tooling (see Limitations). Only MLP gate, up, and down projections are quantized; attention weights and the LM head remain BF16.

Baselines.

Five external methods: RTN (Krishnamoorthi, 2018), GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023), AWQ (Lin et al., 2024), and AutoRound (Cheng et al., 2023), all at W4A16 g128 (≈4.1\approx 4.1 bpw); SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2023) W8A8 (≈8.1\approx 8.1 bpw). SmoothQuant eval mode: weights are smoothed and fake-quantized to int8 then restored to BF16; activations stay BF16. All comparisons against SmoothQuant in this paper are on weight storage and memory bandwidth, not matmul arithmetic.

QAM-W variants.

QAM-W-polar (polar baseline, ≈4.0\approx 4.0 bpw), QAM-W-4 (joint 2D, B=8B\!=\!8, ≈4.0\approx 4.0 bpw), and QAM-W-5.5 (joint 2D, B=11B\!=\!11, AWQ-style scaling α=0.3\alpha\!=\!0.3, ≈5.5\approx 5.5 bpw). A sub-4 bpw variant QAM-W-3.5 (B=7B\!=\!7, ≈3.5\approx 3.5 bpw) is reported in section 5.3.1.

Metrics.

WikiText-2 (Merity et al., 2017) stride perplexity (seq_len 2048, stride 1024, 16K scored tokens); paired KL divergence against BF16 (4K scored tokens); six-task lm-evaluation-harness (Gao et al., 2024) panel (PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), COPA (Roemmele et al., 2011), RTE (Wang et al., 2018), OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018), LAMBADA-OpenAI (Paperno et al., 2016)). Full reproducibility details including model SHAs, calibration setup, and hardware are in appendix J.

5.1 Cross-Model Quality Results

Table 1 summarizes the cross-model quality story.

QAM-W-5.5 reaches the BF16 envelope at the lowest bitrate.

At ≈5.5\approx 5.5 bpw, QAM-W-5.5 stays within ±0.4%\pm 0.4\% of BF16 perplexity on all three models. SmoothQuant W8A8 reaches the same envelope but at ≈8.1\approx 8.1 bpw — about 47%47\% more weight bits.

Calibration narrows the cross-model spread. Uncalibrated RTN costs +1.9% on Mistral 7B but +24.6% on Qwen 2.5 3B — a 12×\times spread driven by architecture alone. Among calibrated methods (GPTQ, AWQ, AutoRound, QAM-W-5.5) the cross-model spread is much tighter. Single-model comparisons among uncalibrated quantizers can therefore mislead in a way that calibrated comparisons typically do not.

Joint 2D coding beats polar at equal bitrate.

At ≈4\approx 4 bpw, QAM-W-4 beats QAM-W-polar by 1–3 pp of Δ\DeltaPPL on the quantization-tolerant models (TinyLlama, Mistral) and by 14.6 pp on the quantization-sensitive Qwen 2.5. The joint codebook captures pair-level correlations that the polar factorization discards; the gain is largest precisely where the model is most sensitive to codec choice.

5.1.1 Cross-Model Slope

Across the 3737 (method, model) rows assembled in this study, paired KL and Δ\DeltaPPL% are rank-correlated at Spearman ρ=0.99\rho=0.99 (fig. 1), consistent with the composite bound in section 4. Multi-seed stride-offset rescoring confirms the ranking is robust (std 0.030.03–0.080.08 pp; appendix G).

5.2 Iso-bpw Frontier Comparison

To position QAM-W against the rotated-codebook frontier, we run an iso-bpw comparison on Llama-2-7B-base (Touvron et al., 2023) against QTIP (Tseng et al., 2024b) (4-bit and 2-bit) and AQLM (Egiazarian et al., 2024) (2-bit), using published HuggingFace checkpoints dequantized to BF16 before scoring under our protocol.

QAM-W-5.5 transfers; QTIP leads at 4 bpw.

QAM-W-5.5 on Llama-2-7B-base reaches +0.29%+0.29\% Δ\DeltaPPL, within the same envelope as the cross-model rows. At iso-4-bpw, QTIP-4Bit (+1.32%+1.32\%, KL 0.0100.010) beats QAM-W-4 (+2.15%+2.15\%, KL 0.0290.029): QTIP’s E8E_{8} lattice trellis and BlockLDLQ rounding outpace QAM-W’s d=2d\!=\!2 Lloyd codebook at a strict 4-bit ceiling. QAM-W-5.5 improves over QTIP-4Bit only at ∼1.4×\sim\!1.4\times the bit budget — a different operating point, not a Pareto win.

Low-bpw frontier.

At ≈2\approx 2 bpw, QTIP and AQLM take comparable PPL hits (+17+17–19%19\%). QAM-W has no 2-bpw operating point; its closest variant is QAM-W-3.5 at ≈3.5\approx 3.5 bpw (section 5.3.1).

5.3 Operating Points and Downstream Behavior

5.3.1 Low-Bit Operating Point: QAM-W-3.5

A B=7B\!=\!7 codebook (128128 codewords) drops QAM-W to ≈3.5\approx 3.5 bpw. On TinyLlama, activation-aware scaling recovers ≈0.5\approx 0.5 bits of effective precision: QAM-W-3.5 (+4.1%+4.1\% Δ\DeltaPPL, KL 0.0370.037) essentially ties the unscaled QAM-W-4 at 4.04.0 bpw (+4.2%+4.2\%, KL 0.0340.034). Without scaling the 7-bit codec costs +7.6%+7.6\%. On Qwen 2.5 the 128-entry codec is not yet Pareto-competitive (+7.5%+7.5\%, worse than GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023) at +2.9%+2.9\%), indicating ∼4\sim\!4 bpw as the lower bound at which the 2D codec geometry pays off on sensitive architectures. On Mistral 7B, 3.5 bpw costs only +1.98%+1.98\%. Full results in appendix E.

5.3.2 Downstream Task Behavior

A six-task lm-evaluation-harness (Gao et al., 2024) panel corroborates the PPL story. LAMBADA is the most quantization-sensitive task; PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020) and COPA (Roemmele et al., 2011) are nearly flat across methods within each model; per-task 95% CI is ±2\pm 2–33 pp at the evaluation limits used, so within-model cross-method differences inside that interval should be read as ties. Per-task breakdowns and Pareto plots are in appendix H.

MMLU.

QAM-W-5.5 and BF16 scored on the full 57-subject MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021) panel match within 0.20.2 pp on all three models (table 3), confirming the codec’s quality envelope extends beyond the perplexity metric.

6 Conclusion

The activation-aware joint-2D variant of QAM-W reaches the BF16 quality envelope at ≈5.5\approx\!5.5 bpw on all five models tested, with Δ\DeltaPPL ≤0.4%\leq 0.4\% on each. Three assumptions underpin the codec: (i) weight-row coordinates are correlated and admit a homogenizing orthogonal rotation; (ii) the rotated pairs concentrate near a circular Gaussian suitable for joint 2D Lloyd coding; (iii) per-channel activation magnitudes provide a rescaling that aligns codec error with the low-eigenvalue directions of MxM_{x}. When any of these weakens — as on Qwen 2.5 3B — all three are needed to recover quality.

In practice, QAM-W-5.5 (≈5.5\approx\!5.5 bpw) is the quality-preserving choice, matching SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2023) W8A8 at ≈32%\approx\!32\% fewer weight bits. QAM-W-4 (≈4\approx\!4 bpw) serves as the iso-bitrate comparison against W4A16 baselines and directly demonstrates that joint 2D coding outperforms polar by 1–3 pp on quantization-tolerant models and by over 14 pp on the most quantization-sensitive one. QAM-W-3.5 (≈3.5\approx\!3.5 bpw) is viable on quantization-tolerant architectures but not yet Pareto-competitive on sensitive ones.

More broadly, among uncalibrated quantizers, sensitivity is dominated by the model architecture: RTN costs +1.9% on Mistral but +24.6% on Qwen, a 12×\times difference from changing the model alone. Among calibrated methods, the spread is much smaller. Single-model comparisons can therefore mislead. Natural follow-ups include a learned 2D codebook fit to each checkpoint’s empirical pair distribution and a fused dequantization-matmul kernel to translate the bitrate saving into inference latency gains.

Limitations

Scope of quantized parameters.

The cross-model headline tables (section 5.1) report bpw over MLP gate/up/down projections only; attention weights and the LM head remain BF16. The MLP + attention extension in section F.1 adds the four self-attention projections (qq, kk, vv, oo) for the BF16 reference and the four strongest sub-8 bpw quantized methods on Mistral 7B and shows the ranking is preserved, but the cross-model tables themselves do not yet include an MLP + attention row for TinyLlama and Qwen; the LM head remains untouched in every reported configuration.

Codebook training cost.

Lloyd-Max codebook training for the joint 2D codec is a one-time cost of ∼5\sim 5 s per bitrate level. This is negligible compared to inference, but it is non-zero and is performed on a synthetic unit circular Gaussian rather than per-checkpoint — a learned codebook conditioned on the empirical post-rotation pair distribution might buy additional precision.

Activation-aware α\alpha is grid-tuned, not learned.

The AWQ-style per-channel scaling exponent α=0.3\alpha=0.3 was chosen from a small grid {0.0,0.3,0.5,0.8}\{0.0,0.3,0.5,0.8\} on TinyLlama and held fixed across models. A per-model or per-layer α\alpha schedule would likely improve quality on Qwen 2.5, where the 7-bit codec is most α\alpha-sensitive.

Architecture coverage.

The cross-model tables rest on three instruction-tuned models from three families (TinyLlama, Qwen 2.5, Mistral) plus two Llama-2 base models at 7B and 13B (sections 5.2 and F.2) — five models from four families across 1.11.1B–1313B parameters. Beyond this range, 7070B and contemporary families (Llama 3, Gemma 2, DeepSeek) would further tighten the architecture-sensitivity claim, particularly to test whether the ≈5.5\approx\!5.5 bpw envelope continues to hold at the 7070B parameter scale where activation statistics diverge further from the smaller-model distributions calibrated against here. The choice to evaluate on these architecturally conventional models is deliberate: all five are dense decoder-only transformers with standard multi-head or grouped-query attention, for which mature weight-loading and evaluation libraries make the codec comparison free of model-loading confounds. Contemporary (2026-era) architectures are not yet reliably supported end-to-end by stock libraries — e.g. Gemma-4 combines per-layer input embeddings with interleaved local/global sliding-window attention and must be loaded through a forked model implementation. Extending QAM-W to such architectures, via a dedicated inference engine, is left to future work.

Iso-4-bpw quality trails the QTIP frontier.

Section 5.2 reports QTIP-4Bit ahead of QAM-W’s joint-2D codec at iso-4-bpw on Llama-2-7B-base; the joint-2D Lloyd codebook trades some rate-distortion ceiling for training cheapness and decode simplicity (a single 2B2^{B}-entry table lookup rather than a lattice nearest-point search). Closing the iso-4-bpw gap is the most natural extension: candidate paths are a richer codebook training distribution per checkpoint (section 6) and tighter Lloyd optimization with QTIP-style BlockLDLQ rounding.

Harness precision.

The six-task harness panel uses limit=300 (Qwen, Mistral) and limit=500 (TinyLlama). The resulting per-task accuracy noise floor is on the order of one to two percentage points; cross-method differences smaller than that should be read as ties.

No fused dequantization-matmul kernel.

The reported bpw is a storage metric. The current pipeline dequantizes weights to BF16 before the linear-layer matmul, so the bitrate saving shows up in weight storage and host-to-device memory bandwidth, not in matmul arithmetic. The bpw numbers should be read as memory-footprint claims until a fused kernel is available. Building this kernel — and with it support for architectures beyond the conventional dense transformers studied here — is the primary engineering follow-up.

Comparison scope.

The evaluation covers five models from four families and seven baselines under one unified protocol. Notably absent are iso-bpw comparisons against learned-rotation methods (QuaRot, SpinQuant) and a direct d=1d\!=\!1 vs. d=2d\!=\!2 ablation against PolarQuant (Vicentino, 2026), which would isolate the codebook-dimension contribution from the shared rotation-plus-scaling pipeline. Scale beyond 13B and broader downstream benchmarks (MMLU-Pro, BBH, IFEval, GSM8K) are also not covered.

Appendix A Codec-Level Analysis

With the encoder/decoder fixed (section 3), the two codec operations that determine directional reconstruction error are the block-Hadamard rotation and the per-pair quantizer. Each is analyzed in turn: the rotation as an exact isometry, and the polar amplitude-phase decomposition as the baseline against which the joint 2D codebook is judged. Layer-output effects — how this directional error translates to perturbations under real activations — are deferred to appendix B.

A.1 Analysis I: Rotation Isometry

The normalized row is transformed by a sign-masked block-Hadamard rotation. This rotation is an exact isometry in real arithmetic, so it cannot add mathematical distortion by itself. Its practical role is to reduce coordinate coherence and spread energy within each block before quantization; the circular-Gaussian model used by the pair codebooks is calibrated empirically and does not follow from orthogonality alone.

Definition A.1 (Unnormalized Walsh-Hadamard matrix).

For any integer b=2mb=2^{m} with m≥0m\geq 0, the unnormalized Walsh-Hadamard matrix Hb∈{−1,+1}b×bH_{b}\in\{-1,+1\}^{b\times b} is defined recursively by H1=[1]H_{1}=[1] and

H2​b=[HbHbHb−Hb].H_{2b}=\begin{bmatrix}H_{b}&H_{b}\\ H_{b}&-H_{b}\end{bmatrix}. (4)

It satisfies Hb⊤​Hb=b​IH_{b}^{\top}H_{b}=bI and Hb=Hb⊤H_{b}=H_{b}^{\top}.

Definition A.2 (Block-normalized Hadamard transform).

Let bb be a power of two dividing dind_{\text{in}}. The normalized block-Hadamard matrix F∈ℝdin×dinF\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}\times d_{\text{in}}} is block diagonal with din/bd_{\text{in}}/b identical blocks, each equal to (1/b)​Hb(1/\sqrt{b})H_{b}:

F=1b​Hb⊕⋯⊕Hb⏟d/b​ blocks.F=\frac{1}{\sqrt{b}}\,\underbrace{H_{b}\oplus\cdots\oplus H_{b}}_{d/b\text{ blocks}}. (5)
Definition A.3 (Sign mask).

Let s1,…,sdin∈{±1}s_{1},\dots,s_{d_{\text{in}}}\in\{\pm 1\} be a deterministic sequence generated from a fixed 64-bit seed. The sign mask is the diagonal matrix S=diag⁡(s1,…,sdin)S=\mathrm{diag}(s_{1},\dots,s_{d_{\text{in}}}).

Lemma 1 (Block-Hadamard rotation isometry).

Assume din=m​bd_{\text{in}}=mb for integers m≥1m\geq 1 and b=2qb=2^{q} with q≥1q\geq 1. Let F=Im⊗b−1/2HbF=I_{m}\otimes b^{-1/2}H_{b} be the block-normalized Hadamard matrix and S=diag⁡(s1,…,sdin)S=\mathrm{diag}(s_{1},\dots,s_{d_{\text{in}}}) with sj∈{±1}s_{j}\in\{\pm 1\}. With Rfwd=F​SR_{\mathrm{fwd}}=FS and Rinv=S​FR_{\mathrm{inv}}=SF, both maps are orthogonal in exact real arithmetic (Rfwd⊤​Rfwd=Rinv⊤​Rinv=IR_{\mathrm{fwd}}^{\top}R_{\mathrm{fwd}}=R_{\mathrm{inv}}^{\top}R_{\mathrm{inv}}=I), mutually inverse (Rinv​Rfwd=IR_{\mathrm{inv}}R_{\mathrm{fwd}}=I), and preserve norms, distances, inner products, and per-block energy.

Proof.

Hb⊤​Hb=b​IH_{b}^{\top}H_{b}=bI and Hb=Hb⊤H_{b}=H_{b}^{\top}, so each normalized block b−1/2Hbb^{-1/2}H_{b} is orthogonal and symmetric. FF is block diagonal with these blocks, giving F⊤​F=IF^{\top}F=I and F⊤=FF^{\top}=F. SS is diagonal with ±1\pm 1 entries, so S⊤=SS^{\top}=S and S2=IS^{2}=I. Then Rfwd⊤​Rfwd=S​F⊤​F​S=IR_{\mathrm{fwd}}^{\top}R_{\mathrm{fwd}}=SF^{\top}FS=I and Rinv​Rfwd=S​F⋅F​S=S​F2​S=IR_{\mathrm{inv}}R_{\mathrm{fwd}}=SF\cdot FS=SF^{2}S=I. Norm, distance, and inner-product preservation follow from orthogonality; per-block energy preservation follows because FF and SS act independently within each block of the partition. ∎

Remark A.1.

The lemma is purely geometric. It proves that the rotation contributes no mathematical distortion and that quantization error has the same Euclidean norm before and after the inverse rotation. It does not prove that the rotated coordinates are independent or Gaussian. If the signs are idealized as independent Rademacher variables, then for a fixed vector vv and coordinate jj in block B⁡(j)B(j),

𝔼S​[(Rfwd​v)j]=0,𝔼S​[(Rfwd​v)j2]=‖vB⁡(j)‖22b.\begin{gathered}\mathbb{E}_{S}[(R_{\mathrm{fwd}}v)_{j}]=0,\\ \mathbb{E}_{S}[(R_{\mathrm{fwd}}v)_{j}^{2}]=\frac{\|v_{B(j)}\|_{2}^{2}}{b}.\end{gathered}

This explains the energy-spreading intuition within each block. Approximate Gaussianity requires the usual incoherence condition that no small number of input coordinates dominates the signed sum, and is checked empirically through calibration.

Remark A.2.

The forward and inverse matrices are generally different because FF and SS do not commute. The sign-masked transform is orthogonal, but it is not generally symmetric and is not generally an involution.

A.2 Analysis II: Polar Pair Distortion

The second codec-level theorem analyzes the polar baseline from section 3. The theorem gives a deterministic amplitude-phase decomposition; the following corollary adds the Rayleigh/Lloyd source model used to compare independent amplitude-phase coding against joint 2D QAM.

Theorem 1 (Polar QAM pair distortion decomposition).

For a complex pair z=a​ei​θz=ae^{i\theta} and reconstruction z^=a^​ei​θ^\hat{z}=\hat{a}e^{i\hat{\theta}},

‖z−z^‖2=(a−a^)2+2​a​a^​(1−cos⁡(θ−θ^)).\|z-\hat{z}\|^{2}=(a-\hat{a})^{2}+2a\hat{a}\bigl(1-\cos(\theta-\hat{\theta})\bigr). (6)

|a​ei​θ−a^​ei​θ^|2\displaystyle|ae^{i\theta}-\hat{a}e^{i\hat{\theta}}|^{2} =a2+a^2−2​a​a^​cos⁡(θ−θ^)\displaystyle=a^{2}+\hat{a}^{2}-2a\hat{a}\cos(\theta-\hat{\theta})

The phase contribution is therefore 2​𝔼​[a​a^]​η​(Np)=2​σk2​Ma​(Na)​η​(Np)2\mathbb{E}[a\hat{a}]\eta(N_{p})=2\sigma_{k}^{2}M_{a}(N_{a})\eta(N_{p}).

For a centroid Lloyd-Max quantizer, Qa​(U)=𝔼⁡[U∣Qa​(U)]Q_{a}(U)=\mathbb{E}[U\mid Q_{a}(U)] on each cell. By the tower property and the centroid identity, and noting that Qa​(U)Q_{a}(U) is σ​(Qa​(U))\sigma(Q_{a}(U))-measurable so it pulls inside the conditional expectation,

Ma​(Na)\displaystyle M_{a}(N_{a}) =𝔼⁡[U​Qa​(U)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[UQ_{a}(U)] (13)
=𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[U∣Qa​(U)]⋅Qa​(U)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbb{E}[U\mid Q_{a}(U)]\cdot Q_{a}(U)\bigr]
=𝔼⁡[Qa​(U)2].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Q_{a}(U)^{2}].

Since 𝔼​U2=2\mathbb{E}U^{2}=2 for the unit Rayleigh law,

CLM​(Na)\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{LM}}(N_{a}) =𝔼​(U−Qa​(U))2\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}(U-Q_{a}(U))^{2} (14)
=𝔼​U2−𝔼⁡[Qa​(U)2]=2−Ma​(Na),\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}U^{2}-\mathbb{E}[Q_{a}(U)^{2}]=2-M_{a}(N_{a}),

which gives Ma​(Na)=2−CLM​(Na)M_{a}(N_{a})=2-C_{\mathrm{LM}}(N_{a}). Finally, the bound 1−sin⁡h/h≤h2/61-\sin h/h\leq h^{2}/6 follows from the Taylor expansion sin⁡h=h−h3/6+O⁡(h5)\sin h=h-h^{3}/6+O(h^{5}), valid for h∈[0,π]h\in[0,\pi] (the remainder is non-negative on this interval since the next term is +h5/120+h^{5}/120 and the series is alternating with decreasing magnitude). Substituting h=π/Nph=\pi/N_{p} gives 2​(2−CLM​(Na))​η​(Np)≤(2−CLM​(Na))​π2/(3​Np2)2(2-C_{\mathrm{LM}}(N_{a}))\eta(N_{p})\leq(2-C_{\mathrm{LM}}(N_{a}))\pi^{2}/(3N_{p}^{2}). ∎

Remark A.3.

The bound is an idealized source-model statement. The implementation uses a finite Rayleigh integration cutoff Rmax=8R_{\max}=8 and f32 codebook levels, so its CLMC_{\mathrm{LM}} is the numerically integrated distortion of that practical codebook. The Rayleigh tail beyond 8​σk8\sigma_{k} is negligible for the reported bit budgets, but the exact equality above should be read as the population calculation for the ideal Rayleigh source and nearest uniform phase quantizer.

A.3 Rotated-Domain Error Accounting

Each complex pair contains two scalar coordinates. Because the inverse rotation is an isometry, the squared error of the unnormalized inverse-rotated direction is the sum of pairwise errors:

‖u−u~‖22=‖Rfwd​u−y^‖22=∑k‖zk−z^k‖2,u~=Rinv​y^.\begin{gathered}\|u-\tilde{u}\|_{2}^{2}=\|R_{\mathrm{fwd}}u-\hat{y}\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{k}\|z_{k}-\hat{z}_{k}\|^{2},\\ \tilde{u}=R_{\mathrm{inv}}\hat{y}.\end{gathered} (15)

If the decoder subsequently normalizes u~\tilde{u} before multiplying by the stored row norm, that final radial projection is a separate step; the equality above applies to the linear inverse-rotation stage.

Corollary 2 (Direction and per-coordinate reporting).

Let each pair error be ek=‖zk−z^k‖2e_{k}=\|z_{k}-\hat{z}_{k}\|^{2}. Before the optional final direction renormalization,

‖u−u~‖22=∑kek,MSEcoord=1d​∑kek=12​meank⁡(ek).\begin{gathered}\|u-\tilde{u}\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{k}e_{k},\\ \operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{coord}}=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{k}e_{k}=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{mean}_{k}(e_{k}).\end{gathered} (16)

If uu and u^\hat{u} are both unit vectors, then the cosine loss is exactly

1−⟨u,u^⟩=12​‖u−u^‖22.1-\langle u,\hat{u}\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\|u-\hat{u}\|_{2}^{2}. (17)
Proof.

The first identity is the rotated-domain error equality above, and the per-coordinate statement only divides by the d=2​#​{k}d=2\,\#\{k\} scalar coordinates. For unit vectors, ‖u−u^‖22=‖u‖22+‖u^‖22−2​⟨u,u^⟩=2​(1−⟨u,u^⟩)\|u-\hat{u}\|_{2}^{2}=\|u\|_{2}^{2}+\|\hat{u}\|_{2}^{2}-2\langle u,\hat{u}\rangle=2(1-\langle u,\hat{u}\rangle). ∎

A.4 Empirical Check of the Circular-Gaussian Model

Corollary 1 and the Lloyd codebook training in section 3.4 both invoke the circular-Gaussian model for the post-rotation pair distribution. Whether this model is a useful idealization of empirical transformer weights is a separable question that can be checked directly. For each of the three target architectures, one representative MLP down_proj matrix is processed with the same pipeline used by the codec: a sign-masked block-Hadamard rotation at b=1024b=1024 block size, per-row unit normalization, and sampling of 50,00050{,}000 rotated complex pairs. The marginal distributions of the magnitude |z||z| are then compared to a fitted Rayleigh law, and of the real part ℜ⁡(z)\Re(z) to a fitted zero-mean Gaussian, via QQ plots (fig. 3).

Figure 3 shows the empirical check: one representative mlp.down_proj matrix per architecture, 50,00050{,}000 rotated complex pairs after the same sign-masked block-Hadamard rotation the codec uses. The body of the distribution tracks the Rayleigh (magnitude) and zero-mean Gaussian (real-part) marginals closely; departures appear only in the far tail, which the Lloyd training implicitly down-weights through the density-weighted MSE objective. The post-rotation distribution is therefore close enough to the circular-Gaussian model that the analytical results based on it are an informative guide to codec behaviour, not a placeholder assumption.

Appendix B Layer Output Error and Activation Awareness

appendix A established that the codec’s reconstruction error is directional and controlled, to first order, by the per-pair Lloyd distortion. Quality at the model level, however, is not measured in weight space directly: a quantized layer is judged by how its output deviates from the BF16 output under the activations it actually sees. This section bridges weight error to layer-output error via a closed-form trace identity, then uses that identity to motivate AWQ-style per-channel scaling.

Notation.

Throughout this and the following sections, M^x=X⊤​X\hat{M}_{x}=X^{\top}X is the unnormalized activation second-moment matrix (X∈ℝn×dinX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{in}}}, with nn activation rows in the calibration batch), and Mx=M^x/nM_{x}=\hat{M}_{x}/n is its per-token-normalized form. Both forms appear; M^x\hat{M}_{x} in finite-sample empirical identities and MxM_{x} when stating per-sample expectations or when referring to a random activation row’s second moment.

B.1 Activation-Weighted Layer Error

Proposition B.1 (Layer output error identity).

Let W,W^∈ℝdout×dinW,\hat{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times d_{\mathrm{in}}} with Δ​W=W−W^\Delta W=W-\hat{W}, and let X∈ℝn×dinX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{in}}} be a row-major matrix of layer-input activation vectors with n≥1n\geq 1. The identity conditions on the same input activations XX being supplied to the original and quantized layer; if earlier quantized layers perturb XX, that propagation effect is outside this single-layer statement. Define the unnormalized activation second-moment matrix M^x=X⊤​X\hat{M}_{x}=X^{\top}X. Then

‖X​W⊤−X​W^⊤‖F2\displaystyle\|XW^{\top}-X\hat{W}^{\top}\|_{F}^{2} =‖X​Δ​W⊤‖F2\displaystyle=\|X\Delta W^{\top}\|_{F}^{2} (18)
=Tr⁡(Δ​W​M^x​Δ​W⊤).\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tr}(\Delta W\hat{M}_{x}\Delta W^{\top}).

With Mx=1n​X⊤​XM_{x}=\frac{1}{n}X^{\top}X, the mean per-sample squared output error is

1n​‖X​Δ​W⊤‖F2=Tr⁡(Δ​W​Mx​Δ​W⊤).\frac{1}{n}\|X\Delta W^{\top}\|_{F}^{2}=\operatorname{Tr}(\Delta WM_{x}\Delta W^{\top}). (19)

Equivalently, for a random activation row x∈ℝdinx\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}} with finite second moment Mx=𝔼⁡[x⊤​x]M_{x}=\mathbb{E}[x^{\top}x],

𝔼⁡[‖x​W⊤−x​W^⊤‖22]=Tr⁡(Δ​W​Mx​Δ​W⊤).\mathbb{E}\left[\|xW^{\top}-x\hat{W}^{\top}\|_{2}^{2}\right]=\operatorname{Tr}(\Delta WM_{x}\Delta W^{\top}). (20)
Proof.
‖X​Δ​W⊤‖F2\displaystyle\|X\Delta W^{\top}\|_{F}^{2} =Tr⁡[(X​Δ​W⊤)​(X​Δ​W⊤)⊤]\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tr}\left[(X\Delta W^{\top})(X\Delta W^{\top})^{\top}\right]
=Tr⁡(X​Δ​W⊤​Δ​W​X⊤)\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tr}(X\Delta W^{\top}\Delta WX^{\top})
=Tr⁡(Δ​W​X⊤​X​Δ​W⊤).\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tr}(\Delta WX^{\top}X\Delta W^{\top}).

Dividing by nn gives the empirical mean. The random-activation statement is the same identity with Mx=𝔼⁡[x⊤​x]M_{x}=\mathbb{E}[x^{\top}x]. ∎

This identity shows that the relevant layer objective is not unweighted weight MSE, ‖Δ​W‖F2\|\Delta W\|_{F}^{2}, but activation-weighted error on the calibration activations. Unweighted MSE is recovered only when MxM_{x} is proportional to the identity. The matrix MxM_{x} is an uncentered second moment; it equals the covariance only when activations have zero mean. The implementation reports the relative layer-output RMSE

‖X​W⊤−X​W^⊤‖F‖X​W⊤‖F,\frac{\|XW^{\top}-X\hat{W}^{\top}\|_{F}}{\|XW^{\top}\|_{F}}, (21)

which is the proposition’s numerator normalized by the BF16 layer-output norm.

Corollary 3 (Diagonal activation-RMS surrogate).

If the normalized activation second moment is diagonal, Mx=diag⁡(r12,…,rdin2)M_{x}=\operatorname{diag}(r_{1}^{2},\ldots,r_{d_{\mathrm{in}}}^{2}), then

1n​‖X​Δ​W⊤‖F2=∑i=1dout∑j=1dinrj2​(Δ​Wi​j)2.\frac{1}{n}\|X\Delta W^{\top}\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}}\sum_{j=1}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}}r_{j}^{2}(\Delta W_{ij})^{2}. (22)

For empirical calibration activations, rj2=n−1​∑t=1nXt​j2r_{j}^{2}=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{n}X_{tj}^{2} is the squared RMS of input channel jj.

Proof.

Substitute the diagonal MxM_{x} into proposition B.1:

Tr⁡(Δ​W​Mx​Δ​W⊤)\displaystyle\operatorname{Tr}(\Delta WM_{x}\Delta W^{\top}) =∑i(Δ​W​Mx​Δ​W⊤)i​i\displaystyle=\sum_{i}(\Delta WM_{x}\Delta W^{\top})_{ii}
=∑i,jrj2​(Δ​Wi​j)2.\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j}r_{j}^{2}(\Delta W_{ij})^{2}.

The empirical formula for rj2r_{j}^{2} is the jjth diagonal entry of n−1​X⊤​Xn^{-1}X^{\top}X. ∎

When MxM_{x} is not diagonal, this expression is a diagonal approximation that ignores cross-channel activation correlations in the current input basis. It still gives the operative AWQ-style intuition: errors in high-RMS channels matter more to the layer output than equal-sized errors in low-RMS channels.

B.2 Activation-Aware Scaling

QAM-W uses AWQ-inspired per-input-channel scaling before quantization. For scaling factors sj>0s_{j}>0 and Ds=diag⁡(s1,…,sdin)D_{s}=\operatorname{diag}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{d_{\mathrm{in}}}),

Wscaled\displaystyle W_{\mathrm{scaled}} =W​Ds,\displaystyle=WD_{s}, (23)
W^scaled\displaystyle\hat{W}_{\mathrm{scaled}} =Quantize⁡(Wscaled),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Quantize}(W_{\mathrm{scaled}}), (24)
W^\displaystyle\hat{W} =W^scaled​Ds−1.\displaystyle=\hat{W}_{\mathrm{scaled}}D_{s}^{-1}. (25)

The implementation sets sj∝rjαs_{j}\propto r_{j}^{\alpha} with α∈{0.3,0.5,0.8}\alpha\in\{0.3,0.5,0.8\}, normalizes the geometric mean of the scales to one, and clamps scales to [1/16,16][1/16,16].

Proposition B.2 (Sufficient-condition model for activation-aware scaling).

Let Es=Wscaled−W^scaledE_{s}=W_{\mathrm{scaled}}-\hat{W}_{\mathrm{scaled}} be the quantization error in the scaled domain, with expectation taken over the quantizer randomness alone for a fixed (deterministic) weight matrix WW. Assume:

  • (A1)

    Scale-invariant distortion: the per-coordinate quantization error satisfies 𝔼⁡[(Es)i​j2]≤ci​j\mathbb{E}[(E_{s})_{ij}^{2}]\leq c_{ij} for bounded constants ci​jc_{ij} that do not depend on the scaling factors s1,…,sdins_{1},\ldots,s_{d_{\mathrm{in}}}.

  • (A2)

    Diagonal activation second moment: Mx=diag⁡(r12,…,rdin2)M_{x}=\operatorname{diag}(r_{1}^{2},\ldots,r_{d_{\mathrm{in}}}^{2}), as in corollary 3.

  • (A3)

    Unclamped power-law scaling: sj∝rjαs_{j}\propto r_{j}^{\alpha} for some α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], with the global geometric-mean normalization absorbed into WW and no per-channel clipping.

Then the de-scaled error Δ​W(s)=W−W^=Es​Ds−1\Delta W^{(s)}=W-\hat{W}=E_{s}D_{s}^{-1} satisfies 𝔼⁡[(Δ​Wi​j(s))2]=𝔼⁡[(Es)i​j2]/sj2≤ci​j/sj2\mathbb{E}[(\Delta W_{ij}^{(s)})^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[(E_{s})_{ij}^{2}]/s_{j}^{2}\leq c_{ij}/s_{j}^{2}, where the equality uses Δ​Wi​j(s)=(Es)i​j/sj\Delta W_{ij}^{(s)}=(E_{s})_{ij}/s_{j} with sjs_{j} deterministic and the inequality is (A1). Under (A2) and corollary 3, the activation-weighted error satisfies

ℰact​(s)=∑i,jrj2​𝔼​[(Δ​Wi​j(s))2]≤∑i,jci​j​rj2sj2.\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{act}}(s)=\sum_{i,j}r_{j}^{2}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[(\Delta W_{ij}^{(s)})^{2}\bigr]\leq\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}\frac{r_{j}^{2}}{s_{j}^{2}}. (26)

Under (A3) the channel factor changes from rj2r_{j}^{2} to rj2​(1−α)r_{j}^{2(1-\alpha)}, attenuating the activation-weighted contribution of high-RMS channels.

Proof.

With WW fixed and the expectation taken over the quantizer randomness only, Δ​Wi​j(s)=(Es)i​j/sj\Delta W_{ij}^{(s)}=(E_{s})_{ij}/s_{j} with sjs_{j} deterministic, so 𝔼⁡[(Δ​Wi​j(s))2]=𝔼⁡[(Es)i​j2]/sj2\mathbb{E}[(\Delta W_{ij}^{(s)})^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[(E_{s})_{ij}^{2}]/s_{j}^{2}. Assumption (A1)—independence of ci​jc_{ij} from ss—is what makes this division valid as a uniform bound across the choice of scales: 𝔼⁡[(Δ​Wi​j(s))2]≤ci​j/sj2\mathbb{E}[(\Delta W_{ij}^{(s)})^{2}]\leq c_{ij}/s_{j}^{2}. Substituting into the diagonal-MxM_{x} identity from corollary 3 (which is (A2)) gives ℰact​(s)=∑i,jrj2​𝔼​[(Δ​Wi​j(s))2]≤∑i,jci​j​rj2/sj2\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{act}}(s)=\sum_{i,j}r_{j}^{2}\mathbb{E}[(\Delta W_{ij}^{(s)})^{2}]\leq\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}r_{j}^{2}/s_{j}^{2}. Under (A3), sj∝rjαs_{j}\propto r_{j}^{\alpha} with global normalization absorbed into WW and no clipping, so the channel factor rj2/sj2r_{j}^{2}/s_{j}^{2} is proportional to rj2​(1−α)r_{j}^{2(1-\alpha)}. ∎

The proposition is a design model rather than a universal guarantee; it describes how (A1)–(A3) interact, and the deployed quantizer satisfies all three only approximately. Real quantizers are nonlinear: codebook boundaries, row renormalization, and non-uniform Lloyd levels all change the effective source distribution, so (A1) fails when the constants ci​jc_{ij} shift with ss under aggressive scaling. Appendix D probes (A1) directly on a representative MLP down_proj layer of Mistral-7B and finds that the median cjc_{j} is essentially flat across α∈[0,0.8]\alpha\in[0,0.8] but the maximum cjc_{j} grows ∼50×\sim\!50\times, so (A1) holds in the bulk and fails in the tail; the deployed α=0.3\alpha=0.3 sits well below the failure regime. Activation-aware scaling is therefore treated as an objective-motivated variant whose behaviour is checked empirically via layer-output RMSE and paired KL rather than asserted from the design model.

B.3 Empirical Check of the Layer-Output Identity

Proposition B.1 is exact, so it does not need empirical validation as a mathematical statement. The operational claim that follows from it — that unweighted weight Frobenius ‖Δ​W‖F/‖W‖F\|\Delta W\|_{F}/\|W\|_{F} is a worse proxy for what the model actually computes than the activation-weighted layer-output RMSE Tr⁡(Δ​W​Mx​Δ​W⊤)/Tr⁡(W​Mx​W⊤)\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}(\Delta WM_{x}\Delta W^{\top})/\operatorname{Tr}(WM_{x}W^{\top})} — does. Table 4 reports both quantities (averaged across the 96 MLP linear layers of Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3) for four methods spanning two orders of magnitude in Δ\DeltaPPL%. The Mx matrices are computed from forward-pass activations of the BF16 reference on eight WikiText-2 sequences of length 2048.

Two observations from table 4 support the operational reading of proposition B.1.

Method-dependent amplification.

The activation-weighting amplification factor amp. med. varies by nearly 2×2\times across the four methods. GPTQ’s Hessian-aware optimization aligns its residual error with low-MxM_{x} directions and earns the largest discount (median ρo/ρw=0.57\rho_{o}/\rho_{w}=0.57): the activation-weighted layer-output RMSE is ∼1.8×\sim\!1.8\times smaller than the unweighted weight Frobenius would suggest. AWQ does not earn the same discount (median 0.950.95): its weight error is roughly isotropic with respect to MxM_{x}, so the activation weighting barely changes the apparent magnitude. SmoothQuant and the activation-aware joint-2D codec sit in between (0.870.87 and 0.830.83 respectively). At equal raw weight Frobenius, two methods can therefore differ substantially on what the model actually computes; weight Frobenius alone is not enough to rank them.

Per-layer spread.

The amplification factor also has substantial within-method spread. For AWQ the per-layer ratio ranges from 0.550.55 to 5.535.53 across the 96 layers (std. 0.500.50); the maximum corresponds to the embedding-adjacent MLP block where the AWQ error happens to project disproportionately onto high-MxM_{x} directions, and the model output inherits the full hit. GPTQ’s per-layer ratio, by contrast, sits in a tight [0.24,0.69][0.24,0.69] band (std. 0.120.12). This is direct evidence that the layer-output identity is doing real work: two layers with the same ‖Δ​W‖F\|\Delta W\|_{F} can produce layer-output error that differs by an order of magnitude depending on how that error aligns with the calibration MxM_{x}. The codec that explicitly accounts for MxM_{x} via per-channel scaling — whether at calibration time (GPTQ) or at quantization time (QAM-W with α=0.3\alpha=0.3) — earns a measurable reduction in ρo\rho_{o} that unweighted Frobenius cannot see.

Appendix C From Codec Error to Model Behavior

Proposition B.1 maps weight error to layer-output error. Appendix A earlier derived per-pair codec distortion. This section closes the chain to model behavior with a local logit-KL bridge, then composes the three steps into a single monotone upper bound whose codec-dependent ingredient is the per-pair Lloyd distortion DBD_{B} on the unit circular Gaussian. The bound is tested empirically in sections 5.1 and 5.3.2: if informative, measured paired KL should be rank-correlated with DBD_{B} across methods at fixed architecture.

C.1 Logit Perturbation and Local KL Bridge

Let f⁡(x)f(x) be the BF16 logits and f^​(x)\hat{f}(x) the logits under quantized weights, with δ=f^​(x)−f​(x)\delta=\hat{f}(x)-f(x). If the transformer computation after the perturbed linear layers is locally Lipschitz around the evaluation activation trajectories, then the logit perturbation is controlled by the accumulated layer-output perturbations,

‖δ‖2≲L​∑ℓ‖Xℓ​Δ​Wℓ⊤‖F.\|\delta\|_{2}\;\lesssim\;L\sum_{\ell}\|X_{\ell}\Delta W_{\ell}^{\top}\|_{F}. (27)

The constant LL is not estimated here because norm-only Lipschitz bounds for transformers are usually too loose to be useful. The structural point is that activation-weighted layer error is the quantity that propagates, not raw weight MSE.

Corollary 4 (Local logit-KL bridge).

Let p=softmax⁡(f)p=\operatorname{softmax}(f) and q=softmax⁡(f+δ)q=\operatorname{softmax}(f+\delta) with logit Hessian Fp=diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤F_{p}=\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^{\top}. Then

DKL(p∥q)=12δ⊤Fpδ+r(δ),D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=\tfrac{1}{2}\delta^{\top}F_{p}\delta+r(\delta), (28)

where the third-order Lagrange remainder satisfies |r⁡(δ)|≤13​‖δ‖23|r(\delta)|\leq\tfrac{1}{3}\|\delta\|_{2}^{3} (proof below; the softmax cumulant tensor’s operator-3-norm on the unit sphere is bounded by 2/2≤1\sqrt{2}/2\leq 1). Since ‖Fp‖2≤1/2\|F_{p}\|_{2}\leq 1/2, the local approximation DKL(p∥q)≈14∥δ∥22D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\approx\tfrac{1}{4}\|\delta\|_{2}^{2} holds with absolute error ≤13​‖δ‖23\leq\tfrac{1}{3}\|\delta\|_{2}^{3}. Combining with (27) gives

DKL(p∥q)≲L24(∑ℓ∥XℓΔWℓ⊤∥F)2,D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\;\lesssim\;\frac{L^{2}}{4}\Bigl(\sum_{\ell}\|X_{\ell}\Delta W_{\ell}^{\top}\|_{F}\Bigr)^{2}, (29)

valid in the regime where the cubic remainder is small relative to the quadratic term.

Proof.

Taylor expansion of softmax cross-entropy around logits ff. The first-order term vanishes because KL is minimized at q=pq=p, and the Hessian is FpF_{p}. The operator-norm bound ‖Fp‖2≤1/2\|F_{p}\|_{2}\leq 1/2 follows from Popoviciu’s inequality applied to a unit-vector random variable under pp. For the cubic remainder, the third-cumulant tensor of the softmax log-partition is Ti​j​k=κ3​(p)i​j​kT_{ijk}=\kappa_{3}(p)_{ijk}. For a unit vector vv and I∼pI\sim p, T⁡(v,v,v)=𝔼p​[(vI−𝔼p​vI)3]T(v,v,v)=\mathbb{E}_{p}[(v_{I}-\mathbb{E}_{p}v_{I})^{3}]. Since ‖v‖2=1\|v\|_{2}=1 we have max⁡v−min⁡v≤2\max v-\min v\leq\sqrt{2}; combining |𝔼⁡[(Y−𝔼​Y)3]|≤(max−min)⋅Var⁡(Y)|\mathbb{E}[(Y-\mathbb{E}Y)^{3}]|\leq(\max-\min)\cdot\mathrm{Var}(Y) with Popoviciu’s variance bound Var⁡(Y)≤(max−min)2/4\mathrm{Var}(Y)\leq(\max-\min)^{2}/4 gives |T⁡(v,v,v)|≤(2)3/4=2/2≤1|T(v,v,v)|\leq(\sqrt{2})^{3}/4=\sqrt{2}/2\leq 1. The Lagrange remainder is r⁡(δ)=16​T​(ξ)​(δ,δ,δ)r(\delta)=\tfrac{1}{6}T(\xi)(\delta,\delta,\delta) for some ξ\xi on the segment, so |r⁡(δ)|≤16​‖δ‖3<13​‖δ‖3|r(\delta)|\leq\tfrac{1}{6}\,\|\delta\|^{3}<\tfrac{1}{3}\|\delta\|^{3}. Substituting (27) into the quadratic term gives the final display. ∎

Remark C.1.

Realized KL can be much smaller than this bound because quantization noise is not necessarily aligned with the leading directions of FpF_{p}. We do not attempt to bound perplexity directly: it depends on the evaluation distribution, token entropy, calibration, and nonlinear error propagation, and any direct bound from ‖Δ​W‖\|\Delta W\| would be too loose to guide codec design. The diagnostic chain (theorem 1 →\to proposition B.1 →\to corollary 4) maps codec to KL; perplexity is reported as the end-to-end metric.

C.2 Composite Bound

Let DBD_{B} denote the per-pair Lloyd-Max MSE of the 2B2^{B}-point planar codebook on the unit circular Gaussian (theorem 1). For a single weight row w∈ℝdinw\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}} with paired coordinates {zk}\{z_{k}\}, each pair has calibrated scale σk\sigma_{k} (section 3.4). Codebook lookup is performed on each pair after rescaling toward the codebook’s source domain.

Assumption C.1 (Linear codec response).

For pair kk with per-coordinate calibration variance σk2\sigma_{k}^{2} from section 3.4 (so 𝔼​‖zk‖2=2​σk2\mathbb{E}\,\|z_{k}\|^{2}=2\sigma_{k}^{2} under the circular-Gaussian model), the per-pair squared reconstruction error scales with σk2\sigma_{k}^{2}: 𝔼​‖Δ​zk‖2≤σk2​DB\mathbb{E}\,\|\Delta z_{k}\|^{2}\leq\sigma_{k}^{2}\,D_{B}, where DBD_{B} is the per-pair Lloyd-Max MSE on the unit circular Gaussian (per-coordinate variance 11) and the expectation is over the quantizer applied to a row drawn from the calibration sample.

This is exact for high-rate Lloyd codebooks applied to scaled copies of a fixed source (Lloyd, 1982; Max, 1960; Gersho and Gray, 1991; Zador, 1982). For empirical post-rotation pairs the assumption is an idealization; the QQ check (fig. 3) supports its accuracy in the bulk and fig. 4 probes its failure modes in the tail.

Summing Assumption C.1 over pairs of a single row and using Parseval (the block-Hadamard rotation is an isometry, so ∑k‖zk‖2=‖w‖2\sum_{k}\|z_{k}\|^{2}=\|w\|^{2} deterministically; in expectation ∑k2​σk2=𝔼​‖w‖2\sum_{k}2\sigma_{k}^{2}=\mathbb{E}\,\|w\|^{2}, hence ∑kσk2=12​𝔼​‖w‖2\sum_{k}\sigma_{k}^{2}=\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\,\|w\|^{2}) gives

𝔼​‖Δ​W‖F2≤12​DB​𝔼​‖W‖F2,\mathbb{E}\,\|\Delta W\|_{F}^{2}\;\leq\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,D_{B}\,\mathbb{E}\,\|W\|_{F}^{2}, (30)

where the expectation on both sides is over the calibration sample and the quantizer. Plugging (30) into the activation-weighted trace identity (proposition B.1, random-activation form, Mx:=𝔼⁡[x⊤​x]M_{x}:=\mathbb{E}[x^{\top}x]) and applying the PSD quadratic-form bound Tr⁡(A​M​A⊤)≤λmax​(M)​‖A‖F2\operatorname{Tr}(A\,M\,A^{\top})\leq\lambda_{\max}(M)\,\|A\|_{F}^{2},

ρℓ2:=𝔼x​[‖x​Δ​Wℓ⊤‖22]≤12​DB​λmax(ℓ)​‖Wℓ‖F2,\rho_{\ell}^{2}:=\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[\|x\,\Delta W_{\ell}^{\top}\|_{2}^{2}\right]\;\leq\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,D_{B}\,\lambda_{\max}^{(\ell)}\,\|W_{\ell}\|_{F}^{2}, (31)

where λmax(ℓ):=λmax​(Mx(ℓ))\lambda_{\max}^{(\ell)}:=\lambda_{\max}(M_{x}^{(\ell)}) and ρℓ\rho_{\ell} is the per-token layer-output RMS at quantized layer ℓ\ell. Summing over the LqL_{q} quantized layers and applying Cauchy–Schwarz,

∑ℓ=1Lqρℓ≤12​DB​Lq​CW,CW:=∑ℓ=1Lqλmax(ℓ)​‖Wℓ‖F2.\begin{gathered}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L_{q}}\rho_{\ell}\;\leq\;\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}\,D_{B}\,L_{q}\,C_{W}},\\ C_{W}:=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L_{q}}\lambda_{\max}^{(\ell)}\,\|W_{\ell}\|_{F}^{2}.\end{gathered} (32)

Composing with corollary 4 gives the composite bound below.

Theorem 2 (Composite codec-to-KL upper bound is monotone in DBD_{B} and CWC_{W}).

Under the assumptions of propositions B.1 and 4, the upper bound on the realized paired KL divergence between the BF16 and quantized models obtained by chaining (31), (32), and corollary 4 is non-decreasing in two scalars: DBD_{B} (the per-pair Lloyd distortion of the codebook on the unit circular Gaussian) at fixed architecture, and CWC_{W} (a model-fixed constant set by the calibration activations and weight norms) at fixed codec.

𝔼DKL(p∥q)≲U(DB,CW),∂U/∂DB≥0,∂U/∂CW≥0,\begin{gathered}\mathbb{E}\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\,\|\,q)\;\lesssim\;U\!\bigl(D_{B},\,C_{W}\bigr),\\ \partial U/\partial D_{B}\geq 0,\;\partial U/\partial C_{W}\geq 0,\end{gathered} (33)

in the local regime where the cubic Taylor remainder of corollary 4 is small relative to the quadratic term.

Proof.

Each of (31), (32), and corollary 4 is monotone non-decreasing in its codec-dependent argument. Composition of monotone non-decreasing maps is monotone non-decreasing, which establishes the partial-derivative sign of UU. ∎

Remark C.2 (Realized monotonicity is empirical, not theoretical).

A monotone upper bound does not prove the realized quantity is monotone in the same parameters. Whether the realized 𝔼​DKL\mathbb{E}\,D_{\mathrm{KL}} tracks the envelope is what section C.3 measures.

Remark C.3 (Quantitative envelope).

The same proof chain, kept under tight Cauchy–Schwarz inequalities and using the worst-case post-quantization Lipschitz constant LL of the transformer along the evaluation trajectory, gives the explicit bound

𝔼DKL(p∥q)≲L2​Lq8CWDB.\mathbb{E}\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\,\|\,q)\;\lesssim\;\frac{L^{2}L_{q}}{8}\,C_{W}\,D_{B}. (34)

This envelope is loose: LL is not directly observable, CWC_{W} involves the per-layer activation top-eigenvalue rather than a tractable diagonal surrogate, and the Cauchy–Schwarz step at (32) discards cross-layer alignment. The empirical block tests only the monotonicity statement; (34) is reported for completeness, not as the headline claim.

Three structural consequences of theorem 2 are testable.

  • (C1)

    Codec dependence is linear in DBD_{B}. At fixed model, the upper bound on 𝔼​DKL\mathbb{E}\,D_{\mathrm{KL}} scales linearly in DBD_{B}. For a 2B2^{B}-point 2D Lloyd codebook at high rate on the unit circular Gaussian source, Zador’s formula (Zador, 1982; Gersho and Gray, 1991) gives DB∼2​G​(2)​ 2−BD_{B}\sim 2\,G(2)\,2^{-B} with hexagonal-lattice constant G⁡(2)=5/(36​3)≈0.0802G(2)=5/(36\sqrt{3})\approx 0.0802, so per additional bit per pair, ln⁡𝔼​DKL\ln\mathbb{E}\,D_{\mathrm{KL}} should decrease by ≈ln⁡2≈0.69\approx\ln 2\approx 0.69; per additional bit per weight (two pair-bits each), the predicted decrement is ≈2​ln⁡2≈1.39\approx 2\ln 2\approx 1.39 (≈0.60\approx 0.60 dex).

  • (C2)

    Architecture enters through CWC_{W}. The only architecture-dependent factor in the envelope is CWC_{W}, which suggests the cross-model sensitivity gradient in table 1 should track CWC_{W}.

  • (C3)

    Activation-aware scaling reduces effective DBD_{B}. AWQ-style per-channel rescaling shrinks the effective Lloyd distortion by a multiplicative factor determined by the alignment between MxM_{x} and the codec’s directional error (proposition B.2). The composite bound’s first-order dependence on DBD_{B} implies that this scaling enters the KL upper bound multiplicatively at the same order.

C.3 Empirical Validation

The composite upper bound implies one quantitative and two qualitative properties of the envelope; this subsection tests whether the realized 𝔼​DKL\mathbb{E}\,D_{\mathrm{KL}} tracks them.

(C1) Rate-distortion slope.

Reading the per-method paired KL across bpw levels (tables 9, 10 and 11), paired KL drops from ∼10−1\sim\!10^{-1} at 4.04.0 bpw (polar) to ∼×10−3\sim\!3\!\times\!10^{-3} at 5.55.5 bpw (activation-aware joint-2D) to ∼10−3\sim\!10^{-3} at 8.18.1 bpw (SmoothQuant W8A8) — roughly two orders of magnitude over four bits of weight, or ≈0.50\approx\!0.50 dex per bit per weight. The upper-bound prediction is 2​log10​2≈0.602\log_{10}2\approx 0.60 dex per bit. The measured slope is shallower than the asymptote, which matches the bitrates in this study (44–88 bpw) being below the high-rate regime where D∼2​σ2​G​(2)​ 2−BD\sim 2\sigma^{2}G(2)\,2^{-B} becomes tight.

(C2) Architecture-fixed ranking.

For each fixed architecture, table 1 shows the same method ranking (SmoothQuant W8A8 ≻\succ QAM-W-5.5 ≻\succ calibrated W4 ≻\succ uncalibrated W4 / polar). The cross-model Δ\DeltaPPL spread, by contrast, varies by an order of magnitude (fig. 2). Theorem 2 motivates this factorization: within-model dependence is on DBD_{B} alone; between-model spread enters only through CWC_{W}.

(C3) Activation-aware shift.

QAM-W-5.5 (5.5 bpw, with activation-aware scaling) sits at lower KL than QAM-W-4 (4.0 bpw, no scaling) in tables 9, 10 and 11; the two methods differ both in bitrate and in scaling, so the comparison is not iso-bpw, but the gap between them is largest on Qwen 2.5 — the model with the largest λmax(ℓ)\lambda_{\max}^{(\ell)} values per proposition B.2.

Joint check.

Figure 1 (main text) plots measured paired KL against measured Δ\DeltaPPL% for every (method, model) row available in the study: 2424 rows from the three instruction-tuned models, 44 from the Stage D Mistral extension (section F.1), 66 from the Llama-2-7B-base frontier comparison (section 5.2), and 33 from the Llama-2-13B-base scale extension (section F.2) — 3737 rows total across six model variants spanning 1.11.1B–1313B parameters and bitrates from 22 to 8.18.1 bpw. The pooled Spearman correlation is ρ=+0.99\rho=+0.99. The envelope being monotone does not prove the realized quantity is, so the observed ρ\rho is evidence that 𝔼​DKL\mathbb{E}\,D_{\mathrm{KL}} tracks the envelope’s ranking on this dataset rather than a guarantee that it must.

Appendix D Empirical Check of Proposition B.2 (Assumption A1)

proposition B.2’s assumption (A1) is that the per-coordinate squared quantization error in the scaled domain, 𝔼⁡[(Es)i​j2]\mathbb{E}[(E_{s})_{ij}^{2}], is bounded by a constant ci​jc_{ij} that does not depend on the per-channel scaling factors sjs_{j}. The proposition uses this to argue that activation-aware scaling shrinks the activation-weighted error from a rj2r_{j}^{2} channel weighting to a rj2​(1−α)r_{j}^{2(1-\alpha)} weighting. The discussion at the end of appendix B flags A1 as the load-bearing assumption and notes that the deployed quantizer satisfies it only approximately.

This appendix tests A1 empirically. The probe is on model.layers.16.mlp.down_proj of Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (din=14,336d_{\mathrm{in}}=14{,}336 channels), and the codec is the same QAM-W joint-2D Lloyd codebook at B=11B=11 used in the deployed QAM-W-5.5 configuration. For each α∈{0.0,0.3,0.5,0.8}\alpha\in\{0.0,0.3,0.5,0.8\}, the per-channel scaling factor sj∝rjαs_{j}\propto r_{j}^{\alpha} is computed (with the geometric-mean normalization and clamp range [1/16,16][1/16,16] used at deployment), the weight matrix is scaled by diag⁡(sj)\operatorname{diag}(s_{j}), quantized, and the per-channel mean-squared scaled-domain residual is measured as cj​(α)=𝔼i​[(Es)i​j2]c_{j}(\alpha)=\mathbb{E}_{i}\,[(E_{s})_{ij}^{2}].

Reading.

A1’s “bounded constant independent of ss” claim holds approximately for the typical channel: the median cjc_{j} varies by less than 1.3×1.3\times across the full [0,0.8][0,0.8] grid, well inside the natural Lloyd-rounding variance. A1 fails in the worst-case tail: the maximum cjc_{j} grows roughly 50×50\times from α=0\alpha=0 to α=0.8\alpha=0.8, because row renormalization concentrates more energy into a few high-magnitude channels as α\alpha grows. The deployed α=0.3\alpha=0.3 is conservative relative to this tail growth (max cjc_{j} at α=0.3\alpha=0.3 is an order of magnitude smaller than at α=0.8\alpha=0.8), and the per-channel clamp range [1/16,16][1/16,16] is never reached at any α\alpha in the tested grid (clamp hit rate is 0% at all four points). So the proposition’s design model remains a reasonable guide for the deployed range, with the caveat that its bound is not uniformly tight against the high-RMS tail.

Scope.

The probe is on a single representative MLP down_proj layer of one model. Whether the same 50×50\times tail-growth pattern holds across layers and architectures is left as empirical follow-up.

Appendix E Low-Bit Operating Point Details

Appendix F MLP + Self-Attention and 13B-Scale Extensions

F.1 MLP + Self-Attention Quantization Extension

The cross-model study reports bpw over MLP weights only — attention projections and the LM head remain BF16. The natural follow-up: if QAM-W and the strongest baselines are extended to also quantize the four self-attention projections (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj), does the bpw-efficiency ranking persist?

The BF16 reference and the four strongest sub-8 bpw configurations from table 11 (SmoothQuant W8A8, QAM-W-5.5, GPTQ, AWQ) are re-run on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 with stage all_linear, quantizing both MLP and self-attention. Everything else is unchanged: identical calibration corpus (128 WikiText-2 sequences for the linear-codec baselines; per-input-channel RMS over the same 128 sequences for QAM-W-5.5), identical PPL / KL protocol, and the same six-task harness panel. The bpw column now reports a substantially larger fraction of the total model.

Ranking is preserved.

The method ordering from table 1 (MLP only) carries over: SmoothQuant W8A8 ≻\succ QAM-W-5.5 ≻\succ GPTQ ≻\succ AWQ. The two low-distortion methods stay within the BF16 envelope (Δ\DeltaPPL ≤0.15%\leq 0.15\%) and SmoothQuant remains tied with BF16 on the harness average.

Where the extra cost goes.

Comparing against the MLP-only Mistral row of table 11, the principal change is in the 4-bit calibrated methods: GPTQ moves from +0.9%+0.9\% to +1.43%+1.43\% (∼0.5\sim\!0.5 pp worse from quantizing attention), and AWQ from +1.8%+1.8\% to +2.88%+2.88\% (∼1.1\sim\!1.1 pp worse). The two low-distortion methods barely change. Attention projections are slightly more sensitive than MLP projections under per-channel scalar quantization, but the 2D joint codebook and 8-bit per-channel calibration both absorb this extra sensitivity without loss.

Implication for bpw accounting.

The bpw column of table 6 is the more representative comparison for memory-bound deployment, since it spans the full weight pool that the inference runtime loads. QAM-W-5.5 retains its ≈1.5×\approx\!1.5\times bpw advantage over SmoothQuant when both are extended to all linear layers, and its quality gap to BF16 remains within the multi-seed noise floor (table 8).

F.2 Scale Extension: Llama-2-13B-base

The natural follow-up question is whether the ≈5.5\approx 5.5 bpw envelope holds at the next scale rung. Base model is Llama-2-13B, accessed as NousResearch/Llama-2-13b-hf (sha 4b54e9fd...). Protocol is identical to the rest of this paper: MLP-only quantization, stride PPL at seq_len=2048\texttt{seq\_len}=2048, stride=1024\texttt{stride}=1024, 16K scored tokens; paired KL on 4K scored tokens; six-task harness at limit=300\texttt{limit}=300.

The 5.5 bpw envelope holds at 13B.

QAM-W-5.5 at 5.5 bpw lands at +0.25%+0.25\% Δ\DeltaPPL with mean KL 0.0030.003 and a harness average 0.0030.003 below BF16 — inside the ∼2\sim\!2 percentage-point harness noise floor at limit=300. Combining across the study, the same codec on five models from four families spans +0.4%+0.4\% (TinyLlama) / +0.3%+0.3\% (Qwen-2.5-3B) / +0.1%+0.1\% (Mistral) / +0.29%+0.29\% (Llama-2-7B-base) / +0.25%+0.25\% (Llama-2-13B-base) — std 0.100.10 pp across the five.

GPTQ W4A16 g128 is unusually weak at 13B.

GPTQ at 4 bpw lands at +5.05%+5.05\% on Llama-2-13B-base — substantially worse than on the smaller panel (TinyLlama +2.6%+2.6\%, Qwen +2.9%+2.9\%, Mistral +0.9%+0.9\%). This is consistent with GPTQ’s per-channel Hessian-aware optimization being sensitive to particular activation outlier patterns; the Llama-2-13B-base appears to have an unusually hostile pattern at W4A16 g128. The harness average for GPTQ (0.73630.7363) is higher than BF16’s 0.73040.7304, which is inside the harness noise floor and should be read as a tie.

SmoothQuant is effectively lossless at 13B.

At ≈8.1\approx 8.1 bpw SmoothQuant W8A8 (eval mode, section 5) lands at +0.02%+0.02\% Δ\DeltaPPL and exactly matches the BF16 harness average. QAM-W-5.5 achieves comparable quality at ≈32%\approx 32\% fewer weight bits.

Appendix G Stride-Offset Robustness of WikiText-2 Perplexity

The single-seed Δ\DeltaPPL numbers in table 1 are deterministic given the manifest’s weight hash and the corpus, but they sample only one stride-window grid over the WikiText-2 test split. To characterize the noise floor of the evaluation itself, the two principal configurations — BF16 and QAM-W-5.5 (the lowest-bpw method inside the BF16-quality envelope on this panel) — are re-scored under three stride-window starting offsets {0,4000,8000}\{0,4000,8000\}. Each offset shifts the window grid by a different amount and produces a near-disjoint sample of the corpus while preserving the 16K scored-token budget. Models and checkpoints are otherwise identical; qam_aware is re-trained from the deployed config so the off=0 row reproduces the single-seed table 1 value within numerical jitter.

Two readings of table 8 matter for how table 1 should be interpreted.

Absolute PPL is noisy; Δ\DeltaPPL is not.

The absolute PPL has std 0.110.11–0.390.39 across offsets — 1–6% of the mean — because different stride-window starts land in different parts of WikiText-2 test, which have different intrinsic difficulty. But the Δ\DeltaPPL% between BF16 and QAM-W-5.5 at the same offset has std of only 0.030.03–0.080.08 percentage points, about an order of magnitude smaller. The codec-quality measurement factors out the corpus-position variation, which is the right behaviour for a method comparison.

Mistral Δ\DeltaPPL is at the boundary of stride noise.

The single-seed +0.1%+0.1\% Δ\DeltaPPL for Mistral in table 1 sits inside the 0.18±0.08%0.18\pm 0.08\% multi-seed mean envelope: the codec degradation is real but at the same order of magnitude as the WikiText-2 stride-sampling noise floor on this model. On TinyLlama (+0.33±0.03%+0.33\pm 0.03\%) and Qwen (+0.26±0.03%+0.26\pm 0.03\%) the Δ\DeltaPPL is several standard deviations above zero and the relative ranking from table 1 is robust.

Tables tables 9, 10 and 11 expand the headline cross-model summary in table 1 into per-architecture detail: bits-per-weight, absolute WikiText-2 perplexity, Δ\DeltaPPL% vs. BF16, paired mean KL on 4K scored tokens, and the six-task harness average. Rows are sorted by ascending Δ\DeltaPPL%; the BF16 reference row is always first. Throughout:  ↓\downarrow lower is better,  ↑\uparrow higher is better. Shaded rows (⋆\star ) are QAM-W (ours).

Appendix J Reproducibility Checklist

This appendix maps the present paper against the NeurIPS reproducibility checklist and provides the exact pointers a third party would need to re-run any reported row.

J.1 Data and Calibration

Evaluation corpus.

WikiText-2 raw test split, obtained via the HuggingFace datasets library; the version is pinned by the SHA-256 of the local cached *.txt file, recorded in each eval JSON’s corpus metadata (wikitext-2-raw-v1.test.meta.json).

Calibration corpus.

GPTQ, AWQ, AutoRound, SmoothQuant: 128 sequences of length 2048 from the WikiText-2 train split. QAM-W activation-aware variants compute per-input-channel RMS over 16 sequences of length 512 from the same WikiText-2 split, via forward-pass capture (section 5, §\lx@sectionsign “Reproducibility details”). QAM-W weight-side pair-scale calibration uses up to 1024 unit-normalized rows per matrix and no activations.

Downstream task panel.

lm-evaluation-harness at versions 0.4.110.4.11 and 0.4.120.4.12 across the study (per-run version recorded in each eval JSON’s harness.framework_version), no chat template, zero-shot. Batch size 1616 for the cross-model main study, 88 for the Stage D extension and Llama-2-7B frontier comparison, and 44 for the Llama-2-13B scale extension (per-run value in harness.batch_size). Six tasks (section 5.3.2); MMLU (57 subjects) added in section 5.3.2 for the two principal configurations.

J.2 Model Provenance

The three instruction-tuned models and the two Llama-2 base models used in this paper are pinned to specific HuggingFace commit SHAs in section 5, §\lx@sectionsign “Reproducibility details”. The two additional pins introduced by the Llama-2 sections:

  • •

    Llama-2-7B-base: NousResearch/Llama-2-7b-hf at 8efe6c9b93655b934e27bd9981e3ec13e55aee9d.

  • •

    Llama-2-13B-base: NousResearch/Llama-2-13b-hf at 4b54e9fdd2ebd8db0901d37b98d3a53bbfaa4503.

The published QTIP and AQLM baselines (section 5.2) are pinned via their HuggingFace repo paths: relaxml/Llama-2-7b-QTIP-4Bit (03aad3088415e5ec98b1e35924719b11e29c7e45), relaxml/Llama-2-7b-QTIP-2Bit, and ISTA-DASLab/Llama-2-7b-AQLM-2Bit-1x16-hf (9746e511b4eecf972af0a2bb3ebd93f2c5f84ecc).

J.3 Software Versions

  • •

    Rust quantization binary (qam-llm-bench): builds are reproducible from cargo build --release against the included Cargo.toml (see section J.7).

  • •

    Python evaluation pipeline (qambench): version 0.1.0, installed via pip install -e qambench[eval].

  • •

    transformers version: 4.45.x for the main run; aqlm version installed via pip install aqlm resolves to the latest compatible release at run time.

  • •

    lm-evaluation-harness: versions 0.4.110.4.11 and 0.4.120.4.12 across the study (drift reflects upstream package updates between the cross-model main study and the later Llama-2 extensions; the exact version is recorded per-row in harness.framework_version).

  • •

    torch: 2.4.0+cu121 for the QTIP dequant bridge (section 5.2); the rest of the pipeline runs against whatever torch is installed in the active venv.

  • •

    quip-sharp / qtip-kernels: built from the Cornell-RelaxML/qtip repository at the train-fixW forward path; the scripts/day10b_qtip_dequant.py script in the companion repo dequantizes QTIP checkpoints to BF16 via the identity-matrix probe described in section 5.2, §\lx@sectionsign “Setup”.

J.4 Hardware

Every row in the paper was produced on a single NVIDIA A100 80 GB on a rented Vast.ai host. The total GPU time consumed across the study — including cross-model main run, Stage D, multi-seed, per-layer diagnostic, prop:aware A1 empirical check, MMLU, Llama-2-7B frontier comparison (including QTIP dequant), and Llama-2-13B scale extension — is approximately 2020 A100-hours. The total Vast.ai cost at the host’s hourly rate was approximately USD 34.

J.5 Per-Method Hyperparameters

Reported in section 5 §\lx@sectionsign “Configurations” and table 7, table 2, table 1, etc., per method. Concretely:

  • •

    RTN / GPTQ / AWQ / AutoRound: W​4​A​16W4A16 group size g=128g=128, symmetric, f16 per-group scales. AutoRound runs 200 SignSGD iterations.

  • •

    SmoothQuant: W​8​A​8W8A8, smoothing strength αsq=0.5\alpha_{\mathrm{sq}}=0.5, 128 calibration sequences.

  • •

    QAM-W: see section 3. Block-Hadamard block size b=min⁡(2⌊log2⁡din⌋,1024)b=\min(2^{\lfloor\log_{2}d_{\mathrm{in}}\rfloor},1024). Activation-aware exponent α=0.3\alpha=0.3, clamped to [1/16,16][1/16,16], geometric-mean normalized to 1 (appendix B).

  • •

    AQLM 2-bit 1×\times16: published checkpoint; in_group_size=8\texttt{in\_group\_size}=8, nbits_per_codebook=16\texttt{nbits\_per\_codebook}=16, num_codebooks=1\texttt{num\_codebooks}=1.

  • •

    QTIP-4Bit / QTIP-2Bit: published checkpoint; trellis L=16L=16, K∈{4,2}K\in\{4,2\}, V=2V=2 (per QTIP authors’ release).

J.6 Determinism

Per-row PPL and KL are deterministic given the manifest’s weights_sha256 hash, the corpus SHA-256, the eval-time torch.bfloat16 dtype, and the harness version. The Δ\DeltaPPL% spread across stride-window starting offsets is reported in table 8 on three offsets {0,4000,8000}\{0,4000,8000\} for two headline configurations on each instruction-tuned model. The Δ\DeltaPPL% std observed there is 0.030.03–0.080.08 percentage points, which is the noise floor for the cross-model rows.
